Phase 1 -- system map: document the analyzed service's components, external
dependencies, and entry points as SystemComponent entries (kind: service, worker, job,
external-dependency, datastore, or entrypoint), each with a stable ID and a
description; record dependencies between components via `depends_on`. Propose every
entry through the `propose_edits` tool, tagged for phase 1 -- free-form text never
changes the artifacts.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.
I'll start by loading the tool schemas and exploring the codebase.
Repo read. Small fixture service: one public read path (`get_value`) through an in-memory cache to a flat-file store, plus a background evictor and an internal write path.

payload_or_id.description: The only client-facing operation: kvstore.api.get_value(cache, key). Delegates straight to Cache.get, converting a StorageError into an 'error'-labeled increment of kvstore_get_value_requests_total before re-raising; every other return path increments 'success'. This counter is the single piece of instrumentation in the whole package, and it cannot distinguish a correct value from a stale one.

In-process in-memory dict cache (kvstore.cache.Cache) fronting Storage. Cache.get consults its own dict first and returns the cached Entry.value if present; only on a miss does it call Storage.get and insert an Entry stamped with inserted_at_ms = time.time()*1000. It never re-checks storage for an already-cached key and never expires anything itself -- both bounding and freshness are delegated entirely to the evictor. Also caches negative lookups (value=None). Exposes items() for the evictor to walk and evict(key) to drop one entry.

Backing key-value store (kvstore.storage.Storage): a single flat text file holding one 'key,value' pair per line. get() linearly scans the file and splits each line on the first comma; put() reads the whole file into a dict, sets the key, mkdirs the parent and rewrites the file whole. Any OSError on either path is wrapped in StorageError. Both operations are O(file size), the rewrite in put() is non-atomic, and the comma/newline delimiting is unescaped.

The local filesystem path Storage is constructed with, holding the flat-file store. External to the service's own code: its existence, readability, writability, free space and durability are properties of the host, and its contents can be changed by anything else with access to the path. A missing file is deliberately not an error -- Storage.get returns None for it, indistinguishable from a genuinely absent key.

Background eviction pass (kvstore.evictor.run_eviction_pass), the sole mechanism that both bounds cache size and lets a cached key ever pick up a newer value from storage. Walks Cache.items() and evicts entries older than TTL_SECONDS=300, returning the count removed so a caller could observe progress. Its expiry comparison mixes units -- `now` is seconds from time.time() while Entry.inserted_at_ms is milliseconds -- so `now - inserted_at_ms` is always a large negative number and the expired condition is never true. The returned count is not recorded by any metric.

The periodic caller that is supposed to invoke run_eviction_pass on a schedule. Referenced by evictor.py's docstring ('a caller (e.g. a scheduler loop)') but not implemented anywhere in this repo -- no code calls run_eviction_pass. Mapped as a distinct component because whether it runs, how often, and whether it is still alive are separate failure surfaces from the eviction logic itself, and neither is observable today.

Internal, non-client-facing write path (kvstore.admin.update_value). Not reachable from external clients. Writes through to Storage.put only: it accepts a Cache argument but never calls cache.evict(key), so a key already resident in the cache keeps serving its old value after a successful write. Uninstrumented -- no counter, no error metric; a StorageError propagates to the caller unrecorded.

The periodic data-sync job described in admin.py and __init__.py as the user of the internal write path. Not implemented in this repo; its schedule, batch size and failure handling are external. Mapped separately because it is the origin of every write, and therefore the origin of the staleness window opened by admin_update_value not invalidating the cache.

prometheus_client 0.26.0 default registry plus whatever scrapes it. Holds the one Counter this service defines, kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}. No HTTP exposition endpoint (start_http_server or make_wsgi_app) is set up anywhere in this repo, so whether these samples reach a scrapeable surface at all is unverified -- every alert recommendation in later phases rests on this dependency being wired up.

event.text:
Phase 1 accepted — nine components recorded in `system-map.yaml`.

**The map**

```
sm-data-sync-job (job) ──► sm-admin-update-value (entrypoint) ──► sm-storage ──► sm-storage-file
                                          └─(holds a Cache ref, never uses it)─┐
client ──► sm-api-get-value (entrypoint) ──► sm-cache (datastore) ─────────────┴──► sm-storage
                    └──► sm-metrics-registry (external)
sm-evictor-scheduler (job) ──► sm-evictor (worker) ──► sm-cache
```

**Read path:** `get_value` → `Cache.get` → dict hit, or miss → `Storage.get` → linear scan of one flat file. **Write path:** data-sync job → `update_value` → `Storage.put` (whole-file rewrite).

Three things I recorded that shape the later phases:

- **The cache has no self-expiry.** Both cache *bounding* and cache *freshness* are delegated entirely to one component, `sm-evictor` — which makes it a single point of failure for two unrelated user-visible symptoms.
- **Two components exist only by reference.** `sm-evictor-scheduler` and `sm-data-sync-job` are named in docstrings but implemented nowhere in this repo — nothing calls `run_eviction_pass` at all. I mapped them anyway: "the scheduler stopped firing" is a distinct failure from "the eviction logic is wrong," and neither is observable today.
- **`sm-metrics-registry` is mapped as an external dependency, not an implementation detail.** The single Counter is defined, but no exposition endpoint (`start_http_server` / `make_wsgi_app`) exists anywhere in the repo. Every alert I recommend in phase 4 rests on that wiring existing — so it gets to be a component that can fail, rather than an assumption.

I also noted, without yet calling them failure modes: `admin.update_value` takes a `Cache` and never invalidates it; `Storage.get` returns `None` for a missing file identically to a missing key; the `put()` rewrite is non-atomic and the `key,value` delimiting is unescaped.

Ready for phase 2 (failure modes) when you are.

Phase 2 -- failure modes: document every way this service can fail as FailureMode
entries, each with a stable ID, a severity (`critical` demands immediate human
intervention and pages; `warning` demands action soon and files a ticket), a
`user_visible` flag, and -- for a user-visible failure -- its upstream causes named by
`caused_by`, each of which must itself be a documented entry with its own severity and
visibility. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for phase 2.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.
Now the failure chains. Working upstream from each user-visible symptom.

payload_or_id.name: get_value serves a value that storage no longer holds
payload_or_id.description: A client calls get_value(key) and receives a value that was superseded by a later write. Because nothing in the read path re-consults storage for an already-cached key and nothing successfully expires entries, the staleness is not a bounded window -- once a key is cached, its value is frozen for the lifetime of the process. Silent: the request returns 200-equivalent and increments outcome='success'.

payload_or_id.name: Absent-key None is cached permanently and outlives the real value
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get stores the result of a miss unconditionally, including value=None. A read that lands before the key exists -- before the data-sync job's first write, or while the backing file is missing -- caches None, and since no entry ever expires that key returns None forever afterwards even once storage holds a real value. Indistinguishable at the API from a legitimately absent key, and counted as outcome='success'.

payload_or_id.name: Process exhausts memory and dies, failing all in-flight requests
payload_or_id.description: The cache dict grows until the process is OOM-killed or allocation fails. Every in-flight request fails, the whole cache is lost, and on restart the service re-warms from storage -- so the symptom is a periodic hard outage whose interval depends on unique-key traffic rate. Note the crash also destroys the metric counters, so the outage erases part of its own evidence.

payload_or_id.name: get_value raises StorageError to the client
payload_or_id.description: A cache miss reaches Storage.get, the read fails, and StorageError propagates out of get_value to the caller. The one failure in this service that is loud today: api.py increments kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome='error'} before re-raising. Affects only keys not already cached, so the error rate understates the breakage -- a hot key served from cache still reports success while storage is entirely unreadable.

payload_or_id.name: Many keys return None at once after a truncated file rewrite
payload_or_id.description: Reads for keys that previously had values start returning None en masse, because the single backing file was left truncated or partially written. Not a partial degradation -- the file is the entire dataset, so one bad rewrite can lose every key written before it. Returns as 'success' at the API, and cached keys keep serving values, so the loss surfaces gradually as those entries are read for the first time.

payload_or_id.name: Key collision or delimiter injection returns another key's value
payload_or_id.description: get_value returns a value that belongs to a different key, or a truncated fragment of the intended one. The flat-file format escapes nothing: a key containing a comma is split at the wrong point by line.partition(','), and a value containing a newline is read back as an extra line -- creating a phantom key while truncating the real value. Silent data corruption; counted as outcome='success'.

payload_or_id.name: Read latency degrades as the backing file grows
payload_or_id.description: Cache misses get progressively slower as the dataset grows, because each one reads and scans the entire backing file. Degradation is gradual and unbounded rather than a discrete break, and it is worst exactly when it hurts most: after a restart, when the cache is empty and every request is a miss.

payload_or_id.name: Same key returns different values depending on which process serves it
payload_or_id.description: The cache is a plain in-process dict, so in any multi-process or multi-replica deployment each process holds an independent view. Combined with the missing write invalidation, a key updated in storage is served old by processes that already cached it and new by processes that have not -- so repeated identical requests flip between values non-deterministically. Conditional on the deployment topology, which this repo does not define; a single-process deployment does not exhibit it.

payload_or_id.name: Write path never invalidates the cached entry
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value takes a Cache parameter and calls only storage.put -- cache.evict(key) exists and is never called from any writer. Every successful write to an already-cached key opens a staleness window that, given the broken evictor, never closes. Critical rather than warning because the condition is not a risk of future damage: each occurrence is a divergence being created right now, and the divergence is permanent.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction pass evicts nothing due to a seconds/milliseconds mismatch
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass compares `now = time.time()` (seconds) against Entry.inserted_at_ms (milliseconds), so `now - entry.inserted_at_ms` is a large negative number that can never exceed TTL_SECONDS. The expired list is always empty and the function always returns 0. This single defect removes the only backstop for two independent user-visible failures -- unbounded growth and unbounded staleness -- and it fails silently: the pass runs, succeeds, and reports doing nothing, which is indistinguishable from a healthy pass over an already-fresh cache.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction pass is never invoked
payload_or_id.description: Nothing calls run_eviction_pass anywhere in this repo -- the scheduling loop is only described in a docstring. Whether it is absent by construction, was never deployed, crashed, or silently stopped firing, the effect is identical to the unit bug and the two are indistinguishable from outside. Independent of the unit bug: fixing the arithmetic changes nothing if no caller exists, and fixing the scheduler changes nothing while the arithmetic is wrong.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction pass dies iterating the cache while requests mutate it
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass builds a list comprehension over cache.items(), a live view of the dict. If a request thread inserts a new entry during that walk, CPython raises RuntimeError('dictionary changed size during iteration') and the pass aborts. Nothing catches it, and the return value that would signal progress is never produced. A scheduler that does not handle the exception loses its loop permanently; one that does retries into the same race. Latent today because the pass is never invoked, and it becomes reachable the moment the scheduler is implemented.

payload_or_id.name: Cache grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: With no working expiry and no size cap, the cache retains one entry per distinct key ever requested, for the process lifetime -- including entries for keys that do not exist. Under sustained unique-key traffic, memory climbs monotonically. Warning rather than critical because the trajectory is slow and the intervention is scheduled work, not a firefight -- but it terminates in a hard outage, so it must be detected on the ramp rather than at the cliff.

payload_or_id.name: Cached keys are never re-read from storage
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get returns on the first dict hit and never consults storage for a key it already holds. On its own this is the intended design; documented as a distinct link because it is the property that converts every invalidation gap above it into an unbounded one. Any fix that gives entries a maximum age -- a working evictor, a TTL check on read -- caps the blast radius of all of them at once, which makes this the cheapest single point of repair in the whole chain.

payload_or_id.name: Cache state is per-process with no shared invalidation channel
payload_or_id.description: The cache is a per-instance dict with no cross-process coordination, so there is no mechanism by which a write or an eviction in one process can affect another. Any future invalidation fix applied only to the writing process leaves every other replica stale, which makes this a trap for the obvious repair of the write-invalidation gap rather than only a failure in its own right.

payload_or_id.name: Storage.get fails with an OSError
payload_or_id.description: Reading the backing file raises OSError -- permissions changed, the mount went read-only or disappeared, a filesystem I/O error, or file-descriptor exhaustion -- and Storage wraps it in StorageError. Reaches the client only on a cache miss, so during a total storage outage the observed error rate is a function of cache hit ratio rather than of severity.

payload_or_id.name: Backing file absent, reported as an empty dataset
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get explicitly checks self._path.exists() and returns None when the file is gone, so a deleted, unmounted, or never-created store is not an error condition at any layer -- it is reported as 'every key is absent'. The most dangerous property in the codebase for detection purposes: total data loss and a legitimately empty result set are the same signal, and the API counts both as outcome='success'.

payload_or_id.name: Storage.put fails with an OSError
payload_or_id.description: A write fails -- disk full, permissions, read-only mount, I/O error -- and StorageError propagates out of update_value to the data-sync job. Entirely uninstrumented: no counter, no log, no metric anywhere on the write path. Whether it is retried, swallowed, or crashes the job depends on caller code that does not exist in this repo, so today a total write outage produces no signal in this service at all while reads continue reporting success.

payload_or_id.name: Filesystem holding the backing file runs out of space
payload_or_id.description: ENOSPC on the write path. Worse here than in a typical service because put() rewrites the entire file rather than appending: a write that runs out of space partway through does not fail cleanly leaving the previous state intact, it can destroy the existing dataset. Also a slow, predictable, and therefore preventable condition -- the one failure in this list that is reliably detectable well before it does damage.

payload_or_id.name: Whole-file rewrite leaves the store truncated or partial
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put reads the whole file into a dict, then calls write_text, which truncates the target before writing. There is no temp-file-and-rename, no fsync, and no lock: a crash, kill, ENOSPC, or overlapping writer during that window leaves the file empty or half-written, losing keys that were successfully stored long ago. The destructive window is proportional to dataset size, so the risk grows with the data it endangers.

payload_or_id.name: Concurrent writers silently discard each other's updates
payload_or_id.description: put() is an unlocked read-modify-write over the whole file. Two writers interleaving both read the same prior state and the second rewrite discards the first writer's key. No error is raised and both callers observe success; the loss is only visible later as a key holding a value that was definitively overwritten. Reachable whenever more than one data-sync worker, or a retry overlapping its own original, is in flight.

payload_or_id.name: Storage format has no escaping for its comma and newline delimiters
payload_or_id.description: Keys and values are written raw into a comma-and-newline delimited format with no quoting, escaping, or validation on either the read or the write side. Any key containing a comma or any value containing a newline silently violates the format's assumptions. This is attacker- and data-controlled rather than infrastructure-controlled: the trigger is the content of the data, so it can be introduced deliberately.

payload_or_id.name: Read and write cost scale linearly with total dataset size
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get reads the entire file and scans it line by line for one key; Storage.put reads it whole, rebuilds a dict, and writes it whole. Both are O(dataset) per single-key operation, with no index and no partial read. This single defect removes the only backstop for two independent user-visible failures -- unbounded growth and unbounded staleness -- and it fails silently: the pass runs, succeeds, and reports doing nothing, which is indistinguishable from a healthy pass over an already-fresh cache.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass is never invoked
payload_or_id.description: Nothing calls run_eviction_pass anywhere in this repo -- the scheduling loop is only described in a docstring. Whether it is absent by construction, was never deployed, crashed, or silently stopped firing, the effect is identical to the unit bug and the two are indistinguishable from outside. Independent of the unit bug: fixing the arithmetic changes nothing if no caller exists, and fixing the scheduler changes nothing while the arithmetic is wrong.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass dies iterating the cache while requests mutate it
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass builds a list comprehension over cache.items(), a live view of the dict. If a request thread inserts a new entry during that walk, CPython raises RuntimeError('dictionary changed size during iteration') and the pass aborts. Nothing catches it, and the return value that would signal progress is never produced. A scheduler that does not handle the exception loses its loop permanently; one that does retries into the same race. Latent today because the pass is never invoked, and it becomes reachable the moment the scheduler is implemented.

payload_or_id.title: Cache grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: With no working expiry and no size cap, the cache retains one entry per distinct key ever requested, for the process lifetime -- including entries for keys that do not exist. Under sustained unique-key traffic, memory climbs monotonically. Warning rather than critical because the trajectory is slow and the intervention is scheduled work, not a firefight -- but it terminates in a hard outage, so it must be detected on the ramp rather than at the cliff.

payload_or_id.title: Cached keys are never re-read from storage
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Static property of the code rather than a runtime condition: it is true continuously, by construction, from the moment the service starts. An alert on it would fire once at deploy and never clear, carrying no information about the running system, and every occasion on which it does damage is already covered by an alert on one of the modes above it (stale reads, negative-cache poisoning). Recorded as a design finding instead -- capping entry age is the single cheapest repair, because it bounds the blast radius of every invalidation gap in the chain at once.
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get returns on the first dict hit and never consults storage for a key it already holds. On its own this is the intended design; documented as a distinct link because it is the property that converts every invalidation gap above it into an unbounded one.

payload_or_id.title: Cache state is per-process with no shared invalidation channel
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: A fixed architectural property, not a condition that can transition from healthy to unhealthy, so there is no state change for an alert to detect. Its user-visible consequence is already covered by the alert on inconsistent cross-process reads. Recorded because it is a trap for the obvious repair of the write-invalidation gap: adding cache.evict() in the writing process leaves every other replica stale, so that fix must be verified against the deployed topology rather than in a single process.
payload_or_id.description: The cache is a per-instance dict with no cross-process coordination, so there is no mechanism by which a write or an eviction in one process can affect another.

payload_or_id.title: Storage.get fails with an OSError
payload_or_id.description: Reading the backing file raises OSError -- permissions changed, the mount went read-only or disappeared, a filesystem I/O error, or file-descriptor exhaustion -- and Storage wraps it in StorageError. Detectable today only indirectly, via the error-labeled request counter one layer up, and only when a cache miss happens to hit it: during a total storage outage the observed error rate is a function of cache hit ratio rather than of severity.

payload_or_id.title: Backing file absent, reported as an empty dataset
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get explicitly checks self._path.exists() and returns None when the file is gone, so a deleted, unmounted, or never-created store is not an error condition at any layer -- it is reported as 'every key is absent'. The most dangerous property in the codebase for detection purposes: total data loss and a legitimately empty result set are the same signal, and the API counts both as outcome='success'.

payload_or_id.title: Storage.put fails with an OSError
payload_or_id.description: A write fails -- disk full, permissions, read-only mount, I/O error -- and StorageError propagates out of update_value to the data-sync job. Entirely uninstrumented: no counter, no log, no metric anywhere on the write path. Whether it is retried, swallowed, or crashes the job depends on caller code that does not exist in this repo, so today a total write outage produces no signal in this service at all while reads continue reporting success.

payload_or_id.title: Filesystem holding the backing file runs out of space
payload_or_id.description: ENOSPC on the write path. Worse here than in a typical service because put() rewrites the entire file rather than appending: a write that runs out of space partway through does not fail cleanly leaving the previous state intact, it can destroy the existing dataset. Marked a metric gap with respect to this service, which has no visibility into the filesystem at all; host-level free-space monitoring may already exist outside this repo, and phase 4 treats confirming that as the action rather than assuming either way.

payload_or_id.title: Whole-file rewrite leaves the store truncated or partial
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put reads the whole file into a dict, then calls write_text, which truncates the target before writing. There is no temp-file-and-rename, no fsync, and no lock: a crash, kill, ENOSPC, or overlapping writer during that window leaves the file empty or half-written, losing keys that were successfully stored long ago. The destructive window is proportional to dataset size, so the risk grows with the data it endangers.

payload_or_id.title: Concurrent writers silently discard each other's updates
payload_or_id.description: put() is an unlocked read-modify-write over the whole file. Two writers interleaving both read the same prior state and the second rewrite discards the first writer's key. No error is raised and both callers observe success; the loss is only visible later as a key holding a value that was definitively overwritten. Reachable whenever more than one data-sync worker, or a retry overlapping its own original, is in flight.

payload_or_id.title: Storage format has no escaping for its comma and newline delimiters
payload_or_id.description: Keys and values are written raw into a comma-and-newline delimited format with no quoting, escaping, or validation on either the read or the write side. Any key containing a comma or any value containing a newline silently violates the format's assumptions. This is data-controlled rather than infrastructure-controlled: the trigger is the content of the data, so it can be introduced deliberately by whatever feeds the sync job.

payload_or_id.title: Read and write cost scale linearly with total dataset size
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get reads the entire file and scans it line by line for one key; Storage.put reads it whole, rebuilds a dict, and writes it whole. Both are O(dataset) per single-key operation, with no index and no partial read. The service therefore has a dataset size beyond which it cannot meet any latency target, and nothing measures where that ceiling is.

payload_or_id.title: Data-sync job stops writing
payload_or_id.description: The periodic job that owns every write to this service fails, is descheduled, or hangs. Storage silently stops receiving updates while every read continues to succeed against increasingly old data. Nothing in this service observes the job's liveness or the age of the newest write, so from inside kvstore a sync job that stopped months ago is indistinguishable from one that ran a second ago.

payload_or_id.title: Metrics are recorded but never reach a scrape target
payload_or_id.description: The Counter is defined and incremented, but no exposition surface (start_http_server, make_wsgi_app, pushgateway) is set up anywhere in this repo, and no wiring exists to confirm one is configured at deploy time. If the registry is not scraped, every alert derived from it is silently absent rather than failing loudly -- and an alert rule that never fires looks exactly like a healthy service. Documented as a critical failure mode in its own right because it is the single condition that disables the entire output of this analysis.

event.text:
Phase 2 accepted — 25 failure modes, 8 user-visible with their upstream chains.

**The user-visible ends (8)**

| Mode | Sev | Detectable today? |
|---|---|---|
| Stale read served | critical | no |
| Negative-cache poisoning | critical | no |
| OOM crash | critical | no |
| StorageError to client | critical | **yes** |
| Mass key loss | critical | no |
| Wrong value returned | critical | no |
| Slow reads | warning | no |
| Inconsistent cross-process reads | warning | no |

One of eight is visible with the instrumentation that exists. The other seven all terminate in `outcome="success"`.

**What the chains showed that reading file-by-file did not**

- **One defect sits under two unrelated outages.** `fm-evictor-no-op-unit-bug` is the sole `caused_by` shared between the staleness chain and the memory-growth chain. The evictor is the only thing that bounds cache size *and* the only thing that ever refreshes a cached value — so the seconds/ms mismatch is a single point of failure for two symptoms that would look unrelated in an incident.
- **The evictor has two independent ways of not working.** I split `fm-evictor-no-op-unit-bug` (arithmetic wrong) from `fm-evictor-not-running` (nothing calls it) deliberately: fixing either one alone changes nothing, and from outside they produce identical evidence. A fix verified against only one of them looks successful and isn't.
- **Two failure modes I found in the chain rather than in the docstrings:**
  - `fm-eviction-pass-crash-concurrent-mutation` — `run_eviction_pass` iterates a live `dict` view while request threads insert, so it will raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`. Latent *only because the pass is never called*; it becomes reachable the moment someone implements the scheduler, i.e. as part of fixing the other evictor bugs.
  - `fm-negative-cache-poisoning` — `Cache.get` caches `value=None`. A read that lands before the first sync write pins that key to `None` permanently. Combined with `fm-storage-file-missing` (a deleted file returns `None`, not an error), a vanished backing store is silently converted into permanent per-key absence — and counted as success.
- **`fm-metrics-not-exposed` is recorded as a critical failure mode, not a caveat.** No exposition endpoint exists in this repo. If the registry isn't scraped, every rule from phase 4 is silently absent, and a rule that never fires is indistinguishable from a healthy service.

**Two exclusions, with reasons recorded:** `fm-cache-never-rechecks-storage` and `fm-per-process-cache`. Both are static properties of the code, true continuously from startup — an alert on either fires once at deploy and never clears. Their consequences are alerted on via the modes above them. I kept them as documented links because the second is a trap for the obvious fix to the first: adding `cache.evict()` in the writing process leaves every other replica stale.

Metric entries (tied to where each is emitted in the code), then set every failure

must name the failure mode(s) it serves and state whether it is a new metric or a

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

payload_or_id.title: Add a result label distinguishing found from absent on the existing request counter
payload_or_id.description: api.py increments outcome='success' for both a returned value and a returned None. Add result='found'|'absent' so the absent rate is a visible series. This is the single cheapest change in the phase -- three lines at kvstore/api.py:32 -- and it converts three silent data-loss modes into detectable ones, because all of them manifest as a step change in the proportion of reads returning None. Cardinality stays bounded at 2x2 series. Alert on the ratio, never on the absolute count, since absent is a legitimate outcome whose baseline rate is workload-dependent.

payload_or_id.title: Gauge the number of live cache entries
payload_or_id.description: Set from len(Cache._entries) on insert and evict. Process RSS from the default collector already shows the memory ramp, but it cannot attribute it to the cache; this makes growth measurable in the unit the fix operates on and gives a threshold that means something. Paired with the eviction counter below it separates the two evictor failures from ordinary load: entries rising while evictions stay at zero is the signature of both, and is visible long before RSS approaches any limit.

payload_or_id.title: Gauge the age of the oldest cache entry
payload_or_id.description: Computed at scrape time as now - min(inserted_at). The sharpest single detector in this analysis: if eviction is working by any mechanism, this value stays under TTL_SECONDS; if it exceeds TTL, eviction is broken regardless of which of the three evictor failures is the cause. It states the invariant directly rather than inferring it from a proxy, and it is the one metric that would have caught the seconds/milliseconds bug on the day it shipped. It also bounds the staleness window as an observable quantity, which is what makes stale reads alertable at all. Compute it in the same units as the TTL it is compared against -- the defect being detected is itself a unit mismatch.

payload_or_id.title: Count cache entry removals, labeled by what removed them
payload_or_id.description: Incremented in Cache.evict with source='evictor'|'writer'. One metric covers two distinct upstream defects because both present as a zero rate on a specific label value: source='evictor' pinned at zero is the eviction pass doing nothing, and source='writer' pinned at zero while writes are occurring is the missing cache.evict() call in update_value. The writer series is the only direct observation of the write-invalidation gap available anywhere -- every other signal for it is inference from the staleness it produces, several hops downstream.

payload_or_id.title: Record the timestamp of the last successfully completed eviction pass
payload_or_id.description: Set at the end of run_eviction_pass, after the eviction loop completes. Liveness for a background worker must be a completion timestamp rather than a run counter: a pass that starts, raises RuntimeError partway through the dict walk, and dies leaves a run counter incremented and the work undone. Staleness of this gauge is the only signal that distinguishes 'the scheduler is not firing' from 'the scheduler fires and the pass evicts nothing' -- two failures with identical downstream evidence and completely different fixes.

payload_or_id.title: Count eviction passes that terminated with an exception
payload_or_id.description: Incremented from an except block wrapping the pass, with reason bounded to an exception-class name. Requires adding error handling that does not exist today -- currently a RuntimeError from mutating the dict during iteration propagates into the caller and is lost. Worth instrumenting before the scheduler is written rather than after: the race is unreachable while nothing calls the pass, so it will first appear during the very change that fixes the other two evictor defects, which is exactly when a new silent failure is most likely to be attributed to the fix and dismissed.

payload_or_id.title: Count cache lookups by hit or miss
payload_or_id.description: Incremented in Cache.get with result='hit'|'miss'. Beyond the usual value of a hit ratio, it calibrates the existing error counter: storage read failures only reach the API on a miss, so the hit ratio is the conversion factor between observed error rate and actual storage health -- without it, a 2% error rate during a total storage outage is uninterpretable. A sustained miss ratio near 1.0 also identifies the unique-key traffic pattern that drives unbounded growth, distinguishing it from a hot working set that happens to be large.

payload_or_id.title: Histogram of end-to-end get_value latency
payload_or_id.description: The user-facing latency SLI, measured at the only client-facing entry point. Kept separate from the storage-level histogram below because they answer different questions: this one says whether users are affected, that one says why. Bucket boundaries should straddle the intended latency target rather than defaulting to the library's, since the degradation being detected is gradual -- a histogram whose buckets are all far above the operating range reports nothing until the problem is severe.

payload_or_id.title: Histogram of storage operation latency by operation
payload_or_id.description: Wraps Storage.get and Storage.put with operation='get'|'put'. Both are O(dataset) full-file operations, so this measures the scaling limit directly and, read against the file-size gauge, shows whether latency is tracking data growth (structural, needs an index) or something external (disk contention). It also exposes the put-side cost, which no user-facing metric can see because writes are not on the client path -- and it is the put duration that sets the width of the non-atomic rewrite window.

payload_or_id.title: Count storage operations by operation and outcome
payload_or_id.description: Incremented in both Storage.get and Storage.put with operation='get'|'put' and outcome='success'|'error'. Closes the largest single hole in the inventory: the entire write path is uninstrumented, so today a total write outage produces no signal anywhere in this service while reads continue reporting success. Add an errno-class label only if it stays bounded (ENOSPC, EACCES, EROFS, EIO) -- the distinction is worth having because ENOSPC on this codebase's whole-file rewrite risks destroying the dataset, whereas EACCES merely fails the write.

payload_or_id.title: Record the timestamp of the last successful write
payload_or_id.description: Set at the end of a successful Storage.put. Detects the failure that produces no errors at all: a data-sync job that stops running writes nothing, raises nothing, and leaves every read succeeding against frozen data. An error counter cannot see this, because the absence of an operation is not an error. Prefer a last-success timestamp over a write-rate counter -- rate alerting on a periodic job requires knowing its schedule, whereas a timestamp only requires knowing the longest acceptable silence, and it survives a scrape gap without producing a false zero.

payload_or_id.title: Gauge the number of keys in the backing store
payload_or_id.description: Set from len(existing) in Storage.put, which already builds the full dict and so can publish this for free. The primary detector for catastrophic data loss: a truncated rewrite drops the key count discontinuously, and because the file is the entire dataset the drop is unmistakable. Alert on relative decrease rather than an absolute floor -- the correct threshold is workload-dependent, but a store that loses a large fraction of its keys between two scrapes is never healthy. This is a leading signal: it moves at the moment of truncation, whereas the user-visible symptom appears only gradually as affected keys are read for the first time.

payload_or_id.title: Gauge whether the backing file exists
payload_or_id.description: Set to 0 or 1 at the self._path.exists() check that Storage.get already performs -- the information exists in the code path today and is discarded. This is the highest-value-per-line item in the phase: the codebase deliberately treats a missing store as 'every key is absent', which makes total data loss and an empty result set the same observation everywhere downstream. One gauge separates them permanently. Also covers the unmounted-volume case, where the path resolves but the data does not.

payload_or_id.title: Gauge the size of the backing file
payload_or_id.description: Sampled on write or at scrape time via stat(). Read alongside the operation-duration histogram it distinguishes structural latency growth from transient slowness, and alongside the key-count gauge it catches a truncation that a key count alone might miss -- a file that shrinks sharply while the key count holds is the signature of value-level corruption rather than key loss. Also the input to any projection of when the dataset will outgrow the single-file design.

payload_or_id.title: Gauge free space on the filesystem holding the backing file
payload_or_id.description: From os.statvfs on the store's directory. Recommended conditionally: node-exporter-style host monitoring commonly covers filesystem free space already, and duplicating it is waste. Confirm first, and adopt this only if the store's filesystem is not already covered, or if it cannot be matched to this service's alerts by label. Worth the check rather than an assumption either way, because ENOSPC is uniquely dangerous here -- the whole-file rewrite means running out of space mid-write can destroy the existing dataset rather than merely failing the write, and it is the one failure in this analysis that is reliably predictable far in advance.

payload_or_id.title: Count records that violate the flat-file format's delimiter assumptions
payload_or_id.description: Requires adding validation that does not exist: on write, reject or count keys containing a comma and values containing a newline; on read, count lines with no comma at all. kind is bounded to those cases. This is the only detector for silent cross-key corruption, which is otherwise indistinguishable from correct operation at every layer above storage. Because the trigger is data content rather than infrastructure state, it can be introduced deliberately by whatever feeds the sync job -- so a non-zero rate here warrants looking at the data source, not the disk. Escaping the format is the actual fix; this metric measures whether the exposure is being exercised in the meantime.

payload_or_id.title: Sample cached entries against storage and count divergences
payload_or_id.description: A periodic task samples a bounded number of cached keys, re-reads each from storage, and increments result='match'|'diverged'. The only direct measurement of the top user-visible failure -- every other signal for staleness is inference from an upstream proxy, and each proxy can be healthy while reads are still stale. It also covers the negative-cache case specifically, where the cached value is None and storage now holds a value. Two constraints: keep the sample small, since each check is a full-file scan, and ensure each process is scraped as a distinct target so per-replica divergence is attributable -- with a per-process cache, a fleet-wide aggregate can hide one bad replica entirely.

payload_or_id.title: Detect and count overlapping writes to the store
payload_or_id.description: Requires a small code change: record the file's mtime and size when put() reads it, re-stat immediately before write_text, and increment when they differ -- another writer completed inside the read-modify-write window. Lost updates are otherwise perfectly silent, since both writers observe success and only the data disagrees later. Adding a lock is the real fix and would make this counter measure contention rather than loss; that is still worth having, because a non-zero rate is also the precondition for the interleaved-rewrite corruption path.

payload_or_id.rationale: Every Storage.get failure raises through get_value and increments outcome='error', because Storage.get is reached only on a cache miss -- so the existing counter detects this mode with no code change, and it is alertable today. The listed recommendations improve attribution rather than detection: a storage-level counter separates read failures from any future error source at the API, and the hit/miss counter makes the observed error rate interpretable as a fraction of the storage traffic that actually occurred.

Upgraded from the phase 2 provisional status. prometheus_client auto-registers PROCESS_COLLECTOR, so process_resident_memory_bytes and process_start_time_seconds already exist without any code in this repo -- RSS growth detects the ramp and a moving start time detects the restart that ends it, which is precisely this mode's user-visible symptom. Alertable with rules alone, subject to the Linux-only caveat on the process collector and to exposition existing at all. The cache-entries gauge remains recommended because RSS says the process is growing without saying the cache is why, which is the difference between paging someone and telling them what to fix.

Static property of the code, true continuously and by construction from process start, so there is no state transition for a metric to observe or an alert to fire on. Every occasion on which it causes damage is covered by an alert on a mode above it -- stale reads and negative-cache poisoning. Recorded as a design finding: capping entry age is the single cheapest repair in the analysis, because it bounds the blast radius of every invalidation gap in the chain at once.

A fixed architectural property rather than a runtime condition that can transition from healthy to unhealthy, so no metric can distinguish 'happening' from 'not happening'. Its user-visible consequence is covered by the divergence check against cross-process reads. Kept in the record because it is a trap for the obvious repair of the write-invalidation gap: adding cache.evict() in the writing process leaves every other replica stale, so that fix has to be verified against the deployed topology rather than in a single process.

Nothing implemented can see this: a stale hit is served from the cache dict, returns normally, and increments outcome='success' identically to a correct hit. The divergence check is the only direct measurement -- it compares cached values against storage and is the sole signal that stays true when every upstream proxy looks healthy. The other three detect the condition earlier and cheaply: oldest-entry age bounds the staleness window as an observable number, the writer-sourced eviction series exposes the missing invalidation, and last-write timestamp catches the frozen-data case where writes stopped entirely.

Invisible today for two compounding reasons: the API counter does not distinguish a returned value from a returned None, and the storage layer does not distinguish a missing file from an absent key. The result label fixes the first and the file-present gauge the second, so the two together turn 'the store vanished and we cached the void' into two independent visible signals. Oldest-entry age catches the precondition -- an entry that should have expired long ago -- and the divergence check catches the specific state where the cache holds None while storage holds a value.

The existing counter records mass data loss as a rising rate of successful requests, which is worse than no signal. The key-count gauge is the primary detector and a genuinely leading one: it drops at the instant of truncation, whereas the user-visible symptom emerges only gradually as affected keys happen to be read for the first time -- a delay during which the damage is silently compounding. The result label gives the confirming downstream signal, and file size distinguishes key loss from value-level corruption.

No implemented metric can distinguish a correct value from another key's value -- both are one increment of outcome='success'. Detection has to happen where the corruption is introduced, by validating the delimiter assumptions on write and counting unparseable lines on read; nothing downstream can recover the distinction once a value has been written into an ambiguous format. Fixing the format by escaping it is the real remedy, and the counter measures whether the exposure is being exercised while that remains outstanding.

No latency metric of any kind is implemented, at any layer -- the service cannot currently answer how long a request takes. The request histogram supplies the user-facing SLI, the storage histogram and file-size gauge together say whether the cause is structural growth in the O(dataset) scan or something external, and the hit/miss counter explains why latency is worst after a restart when every request is a miss.

Not detectable today, and notably not detectable from aggregates even after instrumentation: divergence confined to one replica disappears into a fleet-wide sum. The divergence check covers it only if each process is scraped as a distinct target so the result can be read per instance, which is why that requirement is written into the recommendation rather than left to the deployment. Conditional on a multi-process topology, which this repo does not define.

The write path emits nothing at all, so the defect is currently invisible at its source and can only be inferred from the staleness it produces several hops downstream. The eviction counter's source='writer' series is the direct observation: pinned at zero while writes are occurring is exactly this defect, stated in one series. That makes it the earliest detectable link in the staleness chain, and it also verifies the fix -- the series going non-zero is proof the invalidation is actually wired, in the process being scraped.

The evictor emits nothing, and the return value that would reveal it -- always 0 -- is discarded by every caller. Oldest-entry age is the decisive detector because it tests the invariant the code is supposed to maintain rather than the code's own report of its work: a pass that succeeds while evicting nothing looks healthy on any counter of runs or errors, but cannot keep entry age below the TTL. Evictions and entry count corroborate. Note the diagnostic asymmetry: these signals are identical to those of the evictor not running at all, so they should page on the shared symptom and leave the two causes to be separated by the pass-liveness gauge.

Nothing observes whether the pass ever runs -- no caller exists in this repo, and if one existed its silence would be indistinguishable from success. The liveness gauge is what separates this from the unit bug: a stale last-success timestamp means the pass is not completing, while a fresh timestamp alongside a rising oldest-entry age means it completes and does nothing. Same downstream evidence, opposite fixes, so both signals are needed to avoid a fix aimed at the wrong defect.

Uninstrumented and, today, unreachable -- nothing calls the pass. It becomes live during the very change that fixes the other two evictor defects, which is the argument for instrumenting it in the same change rather than after: a RuntimeError from the dict-mutation race would otherwise present as the fix silently not working. The failure counter names the cause, the liveness gauge shows the pass stopped completing, and oldest-entry age shows the user-facing consequence.

Not upgraded to alertable even though process RSS is implemented and does track the ramp, because RSS cannot attribute growth to the cache: a leak elsewhere produces the same curve, and the threshold that matters is expressed in entries and entry age rather than bytes. Deliberate split from the OOM crash it causes, which is alertable on RSS -- the crash is a symptom any memory signal detects, whereas catching this on the ramp requires knowing that the cache specifically is what is growing.

The most consequential gap in the inventory relative to its cost. Storage.get already evaluates path.exists() and throws the answer away, so one gauge at an existing branch permanently separates total data loss from a legitimately empty result set -- a distinction that is currently unrecoverable at every layer above storage and is actively misreported as success at the API. The result label and key count give independent confirmation from the read and write sides.

The write path has no instrumentation whatsoever -- no counter, no log, no metric -- so a total write outage produces literally no signal in this service while reads continue reporting success. The operations counter closes the error case. The last-write timestamp is needed as well because the two failure shapes differ: writes failing loudly show up as errors, whereas writes never being attempted show up only as silence, and no error counter can distinguish silence from health.

This service has no visibility into the filesystem at all. Host-level free-space monitoring very likely exists outside this repo, so the recommendation is deliberately conditional -- confirm coverage of this specific path and that it can be joined to this service by label, and only instrument in-process if it cannot. Flagged as a gap rather than assumed covered because ENOSPC is uniquely destructive against a whole-file rewrite, and because it is the one failure here that is reliably predictable far enough in advance to prevent rather than merely detect.

Undetectable today; the corruption is written successfully by definition, so no error path is involved. Key count and file size are the observable evidence of the event itself, while the write-conflict and operation counters cover the two ways it is triggered -- an overlapping writer and a failed write. Detection here is worth the effort despite the real fix being atomic writes, because this mode destroys data that was durably stored long before the failing operation ran.

Perfectly silent today: both writers observe success and only the data disagrees, later, with no error and no anomaly at any layer. Detecting it requires deliberately looking for the overlap -- re-stat the file before writing and compare -- because nothing about a lost update is observable after the fact. The duration histogram is supporting evidence, since the width of the read-modify-write window is what makes the overlap likely, and that window grows with the dataset.

No validation and no metric exist on either the read or the write side, so a record that violates the format is stored and served exactly like a valid one. Phase 3 accepted: 2 metrics inventoried, 19 recommendations, 25 coverage verdicts, 1 phase-2 amendment.

**What's actually implemented**

| Metric | Where declared |
|---|---|
| `kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}` | `kvstore/api.py:19-23` — the only metric authored in this repo |
| `process_*` / `python_*` collectors | prometheus_client's default registry, auto-registered on import |

The second one is worth flagging: I inventoried it because it is genuinely emitted and it changed a verdict. `PROCESS_COLLECTOR` gives `process_resident_memory_bytes` and `process_start_time_seconds` for free, which is enough to detect the OOM crash and the restart. That's the amendment I filed against phase 2 — and I deliberately did **not** extend it to `fm-cache-unbounded-growth`, because RSS proves the process is growing without proving the cache is why.

**Final coverage: 3 alertable, 20 metric-gap, 2 excluded.**

The three alertable ones all rest on the single existing counter plus the free process collector. One is a correction in the *other* direction: I had assumed the error counter under-detects storage read failures, but `Storage.get` is only ever called on a cache miss — so every storage read failure does reach the counter. Its weakness is proportionality, not detection, which changes the alert rule (fire on any sustained non-zero rate, not on a percentage threshold).

**The recommendations that carry the most weight**

- **`mr-storage-file-present`** — highest value per line in the phase. `Storage.get` already evaluates `path.exists()` and discards the answer. One gauge at an existing branch permanently separates total data loss from an empty result set, a distinction currently unrecoverable everywhere above storage.
- **`mr-get-value-result-label`** — the only `change` rather than `new`. Three lines at `api.py:32` splitting `success` into found/absent, which makes three silent data-loss modes detectable at once.
- **`mr-cache-oldest-entry-age`** — tests the invariant rather than the code's self-report. An eviction pass that succeeds while evicting nothing looks healthy on any counter of runs or errors, but cannot hold entry age below the TTL. This is the metric that would have caught the seconds/ms bug on day one.
- **`mr-cache-evictions-total{source}`** — one metric, two unrelated defects, because both appear as a zero rate on a specific label value: `source="evictor"` for the dead pass, `source="writer"` for the missing invalidation.

**One structural finding:** `fm-metrics-not-exposed` is the top priority, because a metrics pipeline's failure cannot be detected by the metrics it carries. Until an exposition surface exists and is confirmed scraped, all three "alertable" verdicts are theoretical. Detection for it has to come from outside the process — target health and the `build_info` gauge.

Phase 4 next: turning these into alert rules, with the paging/ticketing split and the diagnostic pairs that separate identical-looking causes.

annotations.summary: No kvstore instance is exposing metrics to Prometheus
annotations.description: Either the service is down or its metrics pipeline is broken -- both demand attention and neither can be detected by the metrics the pipeline carries, which is why this rule is written on absent() rather than on any kvstore series. It is the precondition for the entire alert set: while it fires, every other rule here is silently unevaluated, and an alert that never fires is indistinguishable from a healthy service. Both halves are needed -- up==1 catches a scrape target that is failing, absent(kvstore_build_info) catches a target that was removed from service discovery entirely and so has no up series to be zero. Verify the exposition endpoint is started at process boot and that the scrape config still matches the job label used here.

annotations.summary: kvstore process is restarting repeatedly
annotations.description: Repeated restarts within an hour, the expected signature of the cache growing until the process is OOM-killed. Deployable today: process_start_time_seconds comes from prometheus_client's auto-registered process collector, so no code change is needed, though the collector is Linux-only. Correlate with process_resident_memory_bytes -- a sawtooth climbing to the same ceiling before each restart confirms memory exhaustion rather than a crash loop from another cause. Note that each restart empties the cache and resets the counters, so the service will look healthy immediately afterwards while the ramp begins again; treat the restart interval, not the current numbers, as the measure of severity.

annotations.summary: The backing store file does not exist
annotations.description: The flat file holding the entire dataset is absent -- deleted, never created, or on a volume that is no longer mounted. Without this rule the condition is invisible by design: Storage.get returns None for a missing file, so total data loss is reported to every layer above it as 'every key is absent' and counted as a successful request. Short for_duration because there is no benign transient version of this: the file either exists or the dataset is gone. Expect reads to keep succeeding from cache while it fires, and expect already-cached keys to poison themselves with None as they are re-fetched -- so recovery requires restoring the file and clearing the cache, not just the former.

annotations.summary: The backing store has lost a significant fraction of its keys
annotations.description: Key count has fallen more than 10% below its 6-hour peak, the signature of a whole-file rewrite that truncated. Because put() rewrites the entire file rather than appending, a single interrupted write can lose keys that were durably stored long before it ran. This is a leading signal and the reason it is worth paging on: the count drops at the instant of truncation, whereas the user-visible symptom appears only gradually, as affected keys happen to be read for the first time and find nothing. Relative rather than absolute threshold because the healthy key count is workload-dependent, but a store shedding a tenth of its keys is never healthy. Restore from backup before the cache masks the extent of the loss.

annotations.summary: Reads are returning 'not found' far more often than normal
annotations.description: The share of reads returning nothing has risen well above its level six hours ago -- the common downstream symptom of three distinct failures: the store's file vanished, a rewrite truncated it, or the cache has pinned None against keys that now have values. Compared against a lagged baseline rather than a fixed threshold because the healthy absent rate is entirely workload-dependent; the additive 0.05 term stops the multiplicative comparison from firing on noise when the baseline rate is near zero. This rule requires the result label to be added to the existing counter -- a three-line change -- and it is the cheapest broad detector in the set. It says something is wrong, not which of the three; pair it with the file-present gauge and key-count rules to discriminate.

annotations.summary: Cached values disagree with the backing store
annotations.description: The sampling check found entries whose cached value no longer matches storage: clients are being served data the store has superseded, and because nothing re-reads a cached key that divergence does not heal on its own. The only direct measurement of the service's top user-visible failure -- every other staleness signal in this set is inference from an upstream proxy, and each proxy can read healthy while reads are still stale. Aggregated by instance deliberately: the cache is per-process, so a fleet-wide sum can hide one bad replica completely. Severity is critical because it serves critical modes, though it also covers the warning-level cross-process inconsistency case.

annotations.summary: Cache entries are outliving their TTL -- eviction is not working
annotations.description: The oldest cache entry is more than twice TTL_SECONDS old, which means eviction is not happening by any mechanism. This tests the invariant the evictor exists to maintain rather than the evictor's own report of its work, which is why it catches all three evictor failures at once -- including the seconds-versus-milliseconds unit bug, where the pass runs, succeeds, reports evicting nothing, and looks identical to a healthy pass over a fresh cache. Consequences are twofold and both permanent: unbounded memory growth and unbounded staleness. IMPORTANT deployment note -- given the current unit defect this fires immediately and never clears. That is a true finding, not a false positive. Ship it at warning severity until the defect is fixed, then raise it to critical; the exit condition is the fix, not a silence.

annotations.summary: No eviction pass has completed recently
annotations.description: The background evictor has not finished a pass within three scheduling intervals: it is not being invoked, or it is dying partway through -- most likely on the RuntimeError raised when a request thread inserts into the cache dict while the pass is iterating it. Deliberately a last-success timestamp rather than a run counter, because a pass that starts, throws, and dies still increments a run counter while leaving the work undone. This is the diagnostic partner of KvstoreCacheEntriesNotExpiring: a stale timestamp here means the pass is not completing, whereas a fresh timestamp alongside a rising entry age means it completes and evicts nothing. Same downstream evidence, opposite fixes. Configure an Alertmanager inhibit rule so this cause suppresses that symptom and one incident pages once.

annotations.summary: Writes to the backing store are failing
annotations.description: Storage.put is raising OSError -- disk full, permissions, read-only mount, or I/O error. Today this failure is completely silent: the write path has no instrumentation at all, so a total write outage produces no signal anywhere in the service while every read continues to report success against increasingly old data. Check the errno label first if it was implemented: ENOSPC is the dangerous case, because put() truncates the file before rewriting it whole, so running out of space mid-write can destroy the existing dataset rather than merely failing the write. Confirm the key count did not drop as well -- if it did, this is data loss, not just a failed write.

annotations.summary: No successful write to the backing store in over an hour
annotations.description: The periodic data-sync job that owns every write to this service has stopped producing them -- failed, descheduled, or hung. Detects the failure shape no error counter can represent: the absence of an operation is not an error, so writes never being attempted looks exactly like a healthy idle service, while reads keep succeeding against frozen data. Set the threshold from the job's actual schedule -- roughly twice its interval -- since 3600s is a placeholder chosen without access to that schedule. This detects that writes stopped arriving, not why; the sync job's own health lives outside this service and should be alerted on by its owner as well.

annotations.summary: Writes are succeeding but no cache entry is ever invalidated by a writer
annotations.description: Writes are landing in storage while the writer-sourced eviction series stays flat at zero -- the direct signature of update_value not calling cache.evict(). This is the earliest detectable link in the staleness chain and the only observation of the defect at its source; everything else is inference from the divergence it produces hops downstream. It also verifies the fix: the series going non-zero is proof invalidation is actually wired in the process being scraped, which matters because the obvious repair only invalidates in the writing process and leaves every other replica stale. Same deployment caveat as the entry-age rule -- this is true today by construction, so ship it at warning until the defect is fixed, then raise to critical.

annotations.summary: The backing store contains records that do not parse
annotations.description: Lines are being read that do not match the key,value format, which means corruption is already in the store rather than being caught at the door. The mechanism is unescaped delimiters: a value containing a newline is read back as an extra line, creating a phantom key while truncating the real value, and a key containing a comma is split at the wrong point. Paged rather than ticketed because the resulting reads are silently wrong -- another key's value returned as this key's, counted as a successful request, undetectable at every layer above storage. Treat the store as untrusted until the affected records are identified; escaping the format is the fix, and until then the corruption can be reintroduced by whatever feeds the sync job.

annotations.summary: Data being written violates the store's delimiter assumptions
annotations.description: Keys containing commas or values containing newlines are arriving at the write path. Ticketed rather than paged because these are caught at the door, before they corrupt the file -- unlike the read-side rule, which fires once the damage is already stored. The distinction is worth preserving in routing: this one is a data-quality problem at the source, and the trigger is data content rather than infrastructure state, so investigate whatever feeds the sync job rather than the disk. Because the content is attacker-influenceable in principle, a sudden appearance after a long clean period deserves a closer look than a steady trickle.

annotations.summary: Overlapping writes are being detected against the backing store
annotations.description: Another writer completed inside a put()'s unlocked read-modify-write window, so the second rewrite silently discarded the first writer's key. Both callers observed success; only the data disagrees, later. Lists only the lost-update mode deliberately, so it stays at warning severity -- the interleaved-rewrite corruption it can also cause is paged on by the key-count and write-error rules, and routing this precursor to a ticket avoids paging twice for one cause. Serializing writes is the real fix, after which this counter measures contention rather than loss and remains worth keeping.

annotations.summary: Cache is growing with no evictions occurring
annotations.description: Entry count has risen over six hours while nothing has been evicted at all -- the cache is accumulating monotonically and will eventually exhaust memory. Ticketed rather than paged because the trajectory is slow and the intervention is scheduled work, but it terminates in a hard outage, so it must be caught on the ramp rather than at the cliff where KvstoreProcessRestartLoop takes over. Expressed in entries rather than resident memory on purpose: RSS shows the process growing without attributing it to the cache, and the threshold that matters is one an engineer can act on. Conjunction of both conditions avoids firing on ordinary warm-up, where entries rise and evictions legitimately lag.

annotations.summary: Eviction passes are terminating with an exception
annotations.description: The pass is raising rather than completing -- expect reason to be RuntimeError, from the cache dict changing size while the pass iterates a live view of it. Warning severity because the mode itself is warning-level and the paging is done by the liveness rule; this one names the cause. Most likely to appear during the change that fixes the other two evictor defects, since the race is unreachable while nothing calls the pass -- which is exactly when a new silent failure is easiest to mistake for the fix not having worked. Snapshot the keys before walking them, rather than iterating the live view.

annotations.summary: p99 get_value latency is above target
annotations.description: Client-visible read latency has degraded. The usual cause here is structural: a cache miss scans the entire backing file, so per-request cost grows linearly with the dataset and there is a size beyond which no latency target can be met. Confirm with the storage duration histogram and file-size gauge -- latency tracking file growth is structural and needs an index, while latency rising against a flat file size points at disk contention or another external cause. Expect this to be worst immediately after a restart, when the cache is empty and every request is a miss. The 0.5s threshold is a placeholder; set it from the actual latency objective, and choose histogram buckets that straddle it.

annotations.summary: Backing file is on track to outgrow the single-file design
annotations.description: Projected from the last 24 hours, the store will exceed 100MB within 30 days. Because both get and put are O(dataset) whole-file operations with no index, file size is the direct determinant of per-request cost on every cache miss and of the width of the non-atomic rewrite window on every write -- so this is a capacity ticket that pre-empts both the latency and the truncation-risk problems. A projection rather than a threshold because the point is to raise it while there is still time to change the storage design, which is not a same-week fix. Set the size limit from measured latency at that size rather than adopting 100MB as given.

annotations.summary: Filesystem holding the backing store is running out of space
annotations.description: Either free space is projected to reach zero within four hours, or there is less than three times the file's own size left. The second clause is the one specific to this codebase: put() rewrites the whole file, so a write transiently needs room for a second full copy, and running out of space mid-rewrite can destroy the existing dataset rather than merely failing the write. That makes ENOSPC uniquely destructive here and worth paging on before it happens -- this is the one failure in the analysis that is reliably predictable far enough ahead to prevent rather than merely detect. If host-level filesystem monitoring already covers this path, use it instead and ensure it routes to this service's owner; do not run both.

The bucket note matters because the degradation is gradual -- a histogram whose buckets all sit far above the operating range reports nothing until the problem is already severe.

payload_or_id.title: Histogram of storage operation latency by operation
payload_or_id.details: Wraps Storage.get and Storage.put with operation='get'|'put'.
payload_or_id.rationale: Both operations are O(dataset) full-file scans, so this measures the scaling limit directly; read against the file-size gauge it distinguishes latency tracking data growth (structural, needs an index) from something external such as disk contention. It also exposes the put-side cost, which no user-facing metric can see because writes are off the client path -- and put duration is precisely the width of the non-atomic rewrite window.

payload_or_id.title: Count storage operations by operation and outcome
payload_or_id.details: Incremented in both Storage.get and Storage.put with operation='get'|'put' and outcome='success'|'error'. Add an errno-class label only if bounded (ENOSPC, EACCES, EROFS, EIO).
payload_or_id.rationale: Closes the largest hole in the inventory: the entire write path is uninstrumented, so today a total write outage produces no signal anywhere in this service while reads continue reporting success. The errno distinction earns its place because ENOSPC against this codebase's whole-file rewrite risks destroying the dataset, whereas EACCES merely fails the write -- same counter, different incident.

payload_or_id.title: Record the timestamp of the last successful write
payload_or_id.details: Set at the end of a successful Storage.put.
payload_or_id.rationale: Detects the failure that produces no errors at all: a sync job that stops writes nothing, raises nothing, and leaves every read succeeding against frozen data. An error counter cannot see this, because the absence of an operation is not an error. A last-success timestamp beats a write-rate counter here -- rate alerting on a periodic job requires knowing its schedule, whereas a timestamp only requires knowing the longest acceptable silence, and it survives a scrape gap without producing a false zero.

payload_or_id.title: Gauge the number of keys in the backing store
payload_or_id.details: Set from len(existing) in Storage.put, which already builds the full dict. Alert on relative decrease rather than an absolute floor.
payload_or_id.rationale: The primary detector for catastrophic data loss: a truncated rewrite drops the key count discontinuously, and because the file is the entire dataset the drop is unmistakable. A leading signal -- it moves at the moment of truncation, whereas the user-visible symptom appears only gradually, as affected keys happen to be read for the first time. The correct absolute threshold is workload-dependent, but a store losing a large fraction of its keys between two scrapes is never healthy.

payload_or_id.title: Gauge whether the backing file exists
payload_or_id.details: Set to 0 or 1 at the self._path.exists() check Storage.get already performs.
payload_or_id.rationale: The highest value per line in the phase: the information exists in the code path today and is thrown away. The codebase deliberately treats a missing store as 'every key is absent', which makes total data loss and a legitimately empty result set the same observation at every layer above storage. One gauge separates them permanently, and it also covers the unmounted-volume case where the path resolves but the data does not.

payload_or_id.title: Gauge the size of the backing file
payload_or_id.details: Sampled on write or at scrape time via stat().

payload_or_id.title: Gauge free space on the filesystem holding the backing file
