payload_or_id.rationale: node-exporter-style monitoring commonly covers free space already and duplicating it is waste -- but confirming is the action, not assuming either way. ENOSPC is uniquely dangerous here because the whole-file rewrite means running out of space mid-write can destroy the existing dataset rather than merely failing the write, and it is the one failure in this analysis that is reliably predictable far in advance.

payload_or_id.title: Count records that violate the flat-file format's delimiter assumptions
payload_or_id.details: On write, count keys containing a comma and values containing a newline; on read, count lines with no comma at all. The kind label is bounded to those cases. Requires adding validation that does not exist.
payload_or_id.rationale: The only detector for silent cross-key corruption, which is otherwise indistinguishable from correct operation at every layer above storage. Because the trigger is data content rather than infrastructure state, it can be introduced deliberately by whatever feeds the sync job -- a non-zero rate points at the data source, not the disk. Escaping the format is the actual fix; this measures whether the exposure is being exercised in the meantime.

payload_or_id.title: Sample cached entries against storage and count divergences
payload_or_id.details: A periodic task samples a bounded number of cached keys, re-reads each from storage, and increments result='match'|'diverged'. Keep the sample small, since each check is a full-file scan, and scrape each process as a distinct target.
payload_or_id.rationale: The only direct measurement of the top user-visible failure -- every other staleness signal is inference from an upstream proxy, and each proxy can look healthy while reads are still stale. It covers the negative-cache case specifically, where the cached value is None and storage now holds a value. The per-target requirement is not incidental: with a per-process cache, a fleet-wide aggregate can hide one bad replica entirely.

payload_or_id.title: Detect and count overlapping writes to the store
payload_or_id.details: Record the file's mtime and size when put() reads it, re-stat immediately before write_text, and increment when they differ -- another writer completed inside the read-modify-write window.
payload_or_id.rationale: Lost updates are otherwise perfectly silent: both writers observe success and only the data disagrees, later. Adding a lock is the real fix and would turn this counter into a measure of contention rather than loss -- still worth having, because a non-zero rate is also the precondition for the interleaved-rewrite corruption path.

annotations.summary: get_value is returning StorageError to clients
annotations.description: The backing store is failing to read and the error is propagating to callers. Deployable today against instrumentation that already exists -- this is the only rule in the set needing no code change. The threshold is deliberately any sustained non-zero rate rather than a percentage of requests: Storage.get is reached only on a cache miss, so during a total storage outage the error ratio tracks the cache miss ratio rather than the severity of the outage, and a service serving 98% of traffic from cache with completely unreadable storage would sit under any sensible percentage threshold. Check the backing file's permissions, mount and filesystem health; cached keys will keep serving successfully throughout, so a quiet success rate is not evidence the store has recovered.

annotations.summary: No kvstore instance is exposing metrics to Prometheus
annotations.description: Either the service is down or its metrics pipeline is broken -- both demand attention and neither can be detected by the metrics the pipeline carries, which is why this rule is written on absent() rather than on any kvstore series. It is the precondition for the entire alert set: while it fires, every other rule here is silently unevaluated, and an alert that never fires is indistinguishable from a healthy service. Both halves are needed -- up==1 catches a scrape target that is failing, absent(kvstore_build_info) catches a target that was removed from service discovery entirely and so has no up series to be zero. Verify the exposition endpoint is started at process boot and that the scrape config still matches the job label used here.

annotations.summary: kvstore process is restarting repeatedly
annotations.description: Repeated restarts within an hour, the expected signature of the cache growing until the process is OOM-killed. Deployable today: process_start_time_seconds comes from prometheus_client's auto-registered process collector, so no code change is needed, though the collector is Linux-only. Correlate with process_resident_memory_bytes -- a sawtooth climbing to the same ceiling before each restart confirms memory exhaustion rather than a crash loop from another cause. Note that each restart empties the cache and resets the counters, so the service will look healthy immediately afterwards while the ramp begins again; treat the restart interval, not the current numbers, as the measure of severity.

annotations.summary: The backing store file does not exist
annotations.description: The flat file holding the entire dataset is absent -- deleted, never created, or on a volume that is no longer mounted. Without this rule the condition is invisible by design: Storage.get returns None for a missing file, so total data loss is reported to every layer above it as 'every key is absent' and counted as a successful request. Short for_duration because there is no benign transient version of this: the file either exists or the dataset is gone. Expect reads to keep succeeding from cache while it fires, and expect already-cached keys to poison themselves with None as they are re-fetched -- so recovery requires restoring the file and clearing the cache, not just the former.

annotations.summary: The backing store has lost a significant fraction of its keys
annotations.description: Key count has fallen more than 10% below its 6-hour peak, the signature of a whole-file rewrite that truncated. Because put() rewrites the entire file rather than appending, a single interrupted write can lose keys that were durably stored long before it ran. This is a leading signal and the reason it is worth paging on: the count drops at the instant of truncation, whereas the user-visible symptom appears only gradually, as affected keys happen to be read for the first time and find nothing. Relative rather than absolute threshold because the healthy key count is workload-dependent, but a store shedding a tenth of its keys is never healthy. Restore from backup before the cache masks the extent of the loss.

annotations.summary: Reads are returning 'not found' far more often than normal
annotations.description: The share of reads returning nothing has risen well above its level six hours ago -- the common downstream symptom of three distinct failures: the store's file vanished, a rewrite truncated it, or the cache has pinned None against keys that now have values. Compared against a lagged baseline rather than a fixed threshold because the healthy absent rate is entirely workload-dependent; the additive 0.05 term stops the multiplicative comparison from firing on noise when the baseline rate is near zero. This rule requires the result label to be added to the existing counter -- a three-line change -- and it is the cheapest broad detector in the set. It says something is wrong, not which of the three; pair it with the file-present gauge and key-count rules to discriminate.

annotations.summary: Cached values disagree with the backing store
annotations.description: The sampling check found entries whose cached value no longer matches storage: clients are being served data the store has superseded, and because nothing re-reads a cached key that divergence does not heal on its own. The only direct measurement of the service's top user-visible failure -- every other staleness signal in this set is inference from an upstream proxy, and each proxy can read healthy while reads are still stale. Aggregated by instance deliberately: the cache is per-process, so a fleet-wide sum can hide one bad replica completely. Severity is critical because it serves critical modes, though it also covers the warning-level cross-process inconsistency case.

annotations.summary: Cache entries are outliving their TTL -- eviction is not working
annotations.description: The oldest cache entry is more than twice TTL_SECONDS old, which means eviction is not happening by any mechanism. This tests the invariant the evictor exists to maintain rather than the evictor's own report of its work, which is why it catches all three evictor failures at once -- including the seconds-versus-milliseconds unit bug, where the pass runs, succeeds, reports evicting nothing, and looks identical to a healthy pass over a fresh cache. Consequences are twofold and both permanent: unbounded memory growth and unbounded staleness. IMPORTANT deployment note -- given the current unit defect this fires immediately and never clears. That is a true finding, not a false positive. Ship it at warning severity until the defect is fixed, then raise it to critical; the exit condition is the fix, not a silence.

annotations.summary: No eviction pass has completed recently
annotations.description: The background evictor has not finished a pass within three scheduling intervals: it is not being invoked, or it is dying partway through -- most likely on the RuntimeError raised when a request thread inserts into the cache dict while the pass is iterating it. Deliberately a last-success timestamp rather than a run counter, because a pass that starts, throws, and dies still increments a run counter while leaving the work undone. This is the diagnostic partner of KvstoreCacheEntriesNotExpiring: a stale timestamp here means the pass is not completing, whereas a fresh timestamp alongside a rising entry age means it completes and evicts nothing. Same downstream evidence, opposite fixes. Configure an Alertmanager inhibit rule so this cause suppresses that symptom and one incident pages once.

annotations.summary: Writes to the backing store are failing
annotations.description: Storage.put is raising OSError -- disk full, permissions, read-only mount, or I/O error. Today this failure is completely silent: the write path has no instrumentation at all, so a total write outage produces no signal anywhere in the service while every read continues to report success against increasingly old data. Check the errno label first if it was implemented: ENOSPC is the dangerous case, because put() truncates the file before rewriting it whole, so running out of space mid-write can destroy the existing dataset rather than merely failing the write. Confirm the key count did not drop as well -- if it did, this is data loss, not just a failed write.

annotations.summary: No successful write to the backing store in over an hour
annotations.description: The periodic data-sync job that owns every write to this service has stopped producing them -- failed, descheduled, or hung. Detects the failure shape no error counter can represent: the absence of an operation is not an error, so writes never being attempted looks exactly like a healthy idle service, while reads keep succeeding against frozen data. Set the threshold from the job's actual schedule -- roughly twice its interval -- since 3600s is a placeholder chosen without access to that schedule. This detects that writes stopped arriving, not why; the sync job's own health lives outside this service and should be alerted on by its owner as well.

annotations.summary: Writes are succeeding but no cache entry is ever invalidated by a writer
annotations.description: Writes are landing in storage while the writer-sourced eviction series stays flat at zero -- the direct signature of update_value not calling cache.evict(). This is the earliest detectable link in the staleness chain and the only observation of the defect at its source; everything else is inference from the divergence it produces hops downstream. It also verifies the fix: the series going non-zero is proof invalidation is actually wired in the process being scraped, which matters because the obvious repair only invalidates in the writing process and leaves every other replica stale. Same deployment caveat as the entry-age rule -- this is true today by construction, so ship it at warning until the defect is fixed, then raise to critical.

annotations.summary: The backing store contains records that do not parse
annotations.description: Lines are being read that do not match the key,value format, which means corruption is already in the store rather than being caught at the door. The mechanism is unescaped delimiters: a value containing a newline is read back as an extra line, creating a phantom key while truncating the real value, and a key containing a comma is split at the wrong point. Paged rather than ticketed because the resulting reads are silently wrong -- another key's value returned as this key's, counted as a successful request, undetectable at every layer above storage. Treat the store as untrusted until the affected records are identified; escaping the format is the fix, and until then the corruption can be reintroduced by whatever feeds the sync job.

annotations.summary: Data being written violates the store's delimiter assumptions
annotations.description: Keys containing commas or values containing newlines are arriving at the write path. Ticketed rather than paged because these are caught at the door, before they corrupt the file -- unlike the read-side rule, which fires once the damage is already stored. The distinction is worth preserving in routing: this one is a data-quality problem at the source, and the trigger is data content rather than infrastructure state, so investigate whatever feeds the sync job rather than the disk. Because the content is attacker-influenceable in principle, a sudden appearance after a long clean period deserves a closer look than a steady trickle.

annotations.summary: Overlapping writes are being detected against the backing store
annotations.description: Another writer completed inside a put()'s unlocked read-modify-write window, so the second rewrite silently discarded the first writer's key. Both callers observed success; only the data disagrees, later. Lists only the lost-update mode deliberately, so it stays at warning severity -- the interleaved-rewrite corruption it can also cause is paged on by the key-count and write-error rules, and routing this precursor to a ticket avoids paging twice for one cause. Serializing writes is the real fix, after which this counter measures contention rather than loss and remains worth keeping.

annotations.summary: Cache is growing with no evictions occurring
annotations.description: Entry count has risen over six hours while nothing has been evicted at all -- the cache is accumulating monotonically and will eventually exhaust memory. Ticketed rather than paged because the trajectory is slow and the intervention is scheduled work, but it terminates in a hard outage, so it must be caught on the ramp rather than at the cliff where KvstoreProcessRestartLoop takes over. Expressed in entries rather than resident memory on purpose: RSS shows the process growing without attributing it to the cache, and the threshold that matters is one an engineer can act on. Conjunction of both conditions avoids firing on ordinary warm-up, where entries rise and evictions legitimately lag.

annotations.summary: Eviction passes are terminating with an exception
annotations.description: The pass is raising rather than completing -- expect reason to be RuntimeError, from the cache dict changing size while the pass iterates a live view of it. Warning severity because the mode itself is warning-level and the paging is done by the liveness rule; this one names the cause. Most likely to appear during the change that fixes the other two evictor defects, since the race is unreachable while nothing calls the pass -- which is exactly when a new silent failure is easiest to mistake for the fix not having worked. Snapshot the keys before walking them, rather than iterating the live view.

annotations.summary: p99 get_value latency is above target
annotations.description: Client-visible read latency has degraded. The usual cause here is structural: a cache miss scans the entire backing file, so per-request cost grows linearly with the dataset and there is a size beyond which no latency target can be met. Confirm with the storage duration histogram and file-size gauge -- latency tracking file growth is structural and needs an index, while latency rising against a flat file size points at disk contention or another external cause. Expect this to be worst immediately after a restart, when the cache is empty and every request is a miss. The 0.5s threshold is a placeholder; set it from the actual latency objective, and choose histogram buckets that straddle it.

annotations.summary: Backing file is on track to outgrow the single-file design
annotations.description: Projected from the last 24 hours, the store will exceed 100MB within 30 days. Because both get and put are O(dataset) whole-file operations with no index, file size is the direct determinant of per-request cost on every cache miss and of the width of the non-atomic rewrite window on every write -- so this is a capacity ticket that pre-empts both the latency and the truncation-risk problems. A projection rather than a threshold because the point is to raise it while there is still time to change the storage design, which is not a same-week fix. Set the size limit from measured latency at that size rather than adopting 100MB as given.

annotations.summary: Filesystem holding the backing store is running out of space
annotations.description: Either free space is projected to reach zero within four hours, or there is less than three times the file's own size left. The second clause is the one specific to this codebase: put() rewrites the whole file, so a write transiently needs room for a second full copy, and running out of space mid-rewrite can destroy the existing dataset rather than merely failing the write. That makes ENOSPC uniquely destructive here and worth paging on before it happens -- this is the one failure in the analysis that is reliably predictable far enough ahead to prevent rather than merely detect. If host-level filesystem monitoring already covers this path, use it instead and ensure it routes to this service's owner; do not run both.

Aggregated by instance deliberately: the cache is per-process, so a fleet-wide sum can hide one bad replica completely. annotations.summary: No successful write to the backing store in over an hour
annotations.description: The periodic data-sync job that owns every write to this service has stopped producing them -- failed, descheduled, or hung. Detects the failure shape no error counter can represent: the absence of an operation is not an error, so writes never being attempted looks exactly like a healthy idle service, while reads keep succeeding against frozen data. Set the threshold from the job's actual schedule -- roughly twice its interval -- since 3600s is a placeholder chosen without access to that schedule. annotations.summary: Writes are succeeding but no cache entry is ever invalidated by a writer
annotations.description: Writes are landing in storage while the writer-sourced eviction series stays flat at zero -- the direct signature of update_value not calling cache.evict(). This is the earliest detectable link in the staleness chain and the only observation of the defect at its source; everything else is inference from the divergence it produces hops downstream. It also verifies the fix: the series going non-zero is proof invalidation is actually wired in the process being scraped, which matters because the obvious repair only invalidates in the writing process and leaves every other replica stale. Same deployment caveat as the entry-age rule -- this is true today by construction, so ship it at warning until the defect is fixed, then raise to critical.

annotations.summary: The backing store contains records that do not parse
annotations.description: Lines are being read that do not match the key,value format, which means corruption is already in the store rather than being caught at the door. The mechanism is unescaped delimiters: a value containing a newline is read back as an extra line, creating a phantom key while truncating the real value, and a key containing a comma is split at the wrong point. Paged rather than ticketed because the resulting reads are silently wrong -- another key's value returned as this key's, counted as a successful request, undetectable at every layer above storage. annotations.summary: Data being written violates the store's delimiter assumptions

annotations.summary: Overlapping writes are being detected against the backing store
annotations.description: Another writer completed inside a put()'s unlocked read-modify-write window, so the second rewrite silently discarded the first writer's key. annotations.summary: Cache is growing with no evictions occurring

Set the size limit from measured latency at that size rather than adopting 100MB as given.
